rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In this world, sight, hearing, communication, and understanding are limited by ordinary obstructions; in the hereafter these barriers disappear, allowing Paradise dwellers to converse with Hell dwellers at will.
rows.anchor: these obstructions would be done away with. Whenever the dwellers of Paradise desire they would be able to converse

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Modern instruments such as telescopes, telephones, television, and remote transmission of bodily sounds already show why such afterlife capacities should not seem astonishing; the next world's laws will differ from this world's.
rows.anchor: In today’s era of scientific advancement, this depiction should not be the slightest amazing for human beings.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Paradise dwellers' question is not a reminder, since the time for reminding has passed; it humiliates Hell's dwellers, whose confession removes any remaining barrier to punishment, and the caller's proclamation signals that punishment's beginning.
rows.anchor: This question posed by the Paradise dwellers obviously cannot be understood as a reminder because its time would have passed.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although readers generally attach the description of those who obstruct God's way to the caller's proclamation, Islahi regards it as a divine explanatory insertion that identifies disbelievers, including Quraysh.
rows.anchor: However, in my opinion, they are an insertion from God.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qur'anic insertions recur elsewhere, including 7:51; they present past or future principles and events as happening now, so readers must notice them to preserve discourse sequence and avoid overloaded interpretations that violate literary and linguistic principles.
rows.anchor: One example can be seen in verse 51 coming up.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Interpreters who reject the insertion must force the ending into the sense 'they disbelieved in the Hereafter,' which Islahi says effectively adds wording to the Qur'an.
rows.anchor: those who have not regarded this verse to be an insertion, they had to go to great lengths to adjust the meaning of the last part

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verb yaṣuddūn can be transitive or intransitive; absent a reason to prefer one, Islahi adopts the transitive sense because it also encompasses the intransitive.
rows.anchor: the transitive meaning should be adopted since it encompasses the latter meaning also.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ʿIwaj can mean any deviation people adopt after leaving God's path, but Qur'anic parallels make it refer here to polytheism's deviation from monotheism's straight path.
rows.anchor: this word alludes to creating deviations of polytheism from the straight path of monotheism.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur'an identifies the ḥijāb as a wall between Paradise and Hell; since Paradise is as vast as the heavens and earth, the wall's length is beyond imagining.
rows.anchor: curtain-wall) here refers to the wall between Paradise and Hell.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Aʿrāf is the plural of ʿurf, first used for the top of a horse's forehead or a rooster's comb, and then for a turret or lookout built high enough to see all sides.
rows.anchor: the topmost part of a horse’s forehead and to the comb of a rooster. From here, this word began to be used for a turret

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur'anic style indicates that the turrets stand on the wall between Paradise and Hell, with both worlds visible from them.
rows.anchor: these turrets and observation posts will be found on the wall erected between Paradise and Hell. From these places, both these worlds would be visible.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In this construction rijāl means prominent and distinguished people; Islahi cites 24:37 and a passage he identifies as verse 33 of al-Aḥzāb, and says 7:48 uses the word for disbeliever leaders.
rows.anchor: the way it occurs here, it refers to prominent and distinguished personalities.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When 'all' follows a mention of groups, it refers only to those already mentioned; here that means the dwellers of Paradise and Hell.
rows.anchor: it becomes a defined noun with regard to its meaning.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sīmā means a sign, as illustrated by 48:29; Qur'an and Hadith say believers and disbelievers will be distinguished on Judgment Day by signs and marks of their deeds.
rows.anchor: on the Day of Judgement believers and disbelievers will be distinct from one another through the signs and effects of their deeds.

rows.speaker: Prophet (sws)
rows.claim: In a report, the Prophet compares recognizing later believers with recognizing white-marked horses, then says his community will shine on Judgment Day by wuḍū marks on their foreheads, hands, and feet.
rows.anchor: The Prophet (sws) then said that the people of his ummah will be recognized on the Day of Judgement by the signs of wuḍū

rows.claim: Equal-deed people cannot plausibly be called distinguished personalities, as Islahi explains that this use of rijāl denotes prominent figures.
